justificacion: QA1 (split): The paper explicitly reports the expert-curated test dataset composition: "we compiled 200 QA pairs" from real-life clinical scenarios, and separately describes the MENST dataset structure with raw pairs (N=1985) and paraphrased pairs (N=23,820) across three sets (Table 3). QA2 (baselines): The paper compares MenstLLaMA against 9 state-of-the-art LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude-3, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Mistral, LLaMA-3, GPT-2, Orca 2, Falcon, Phi3), well exceeding the requirement for two or more baselines. QA3 (hyperparams): The paper provides complete fine-tuning hyperparameters: learning rate (2×10⁻⁴), batch size (implicit from 4-bit quantization setup), epochs (5), warmup ratio (0.03), maximum gradient norm (0.3), optimizer (Paged AdamW), and LoRA-specific parameters including maximum sequence length (2048 tokens), quantization (NF4 4-bit). QA4 (dataset): The MENST dataset is fully characterized: name (MENST), domain and task context (menstrual health education with 23,820 QA pairs covering 7 primary topics and 19 subtopics), and explicit size (23,820 paraphrased pairs from 1,985 raw pairs, broken down across 3 sets in Table 3).

QA1 (1.0): The paper explicitly reports the data split: 643 prompt-response pairs total, with 20 questions retained for evaluation after extraction from authentic exam sheets. The fine-tuning dataset composition is clearly stated in Section 2.2. QA2 (0.5): Only one primary baseline is compared—the base model (mistral-base) without fine-tuning. Although GPT-4 and Llama-3.1 serve as evaluators, not alternative methods competing with LoRA. No comparison against other fine-tuning techniques or published baselines is provided. QA3 (1.0): Complete hyperparameter reporting including: LoRA rank=8, lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0.1, batch size=1 with gradient accumulation=4 (effective batch size 4), learning rate implied in "per-device batch size", max epochs=10 (stopped at 6 due to early stopping with patience=2), float32 precision, sequence length=1024 tokens. All PEFT-specific parameters (rank, alpha, dropout) are explicitly stated. QA4 (1.0): Dataset fully characterized: (a) name/source: "authentic university-level computer science examinations" with "20 open-ended questions" from "instructor-validated answers"; (b) domain and task: undergraduate computer science course covering "programming, artificial intelligence, and data-driven reasoning"; (c) size: 643 prompt-response pairs for fine-tuning, 20 questions for evaluation, with rubric annotations across technical and argumentative categories.

QA1: The paper explicitly reports train/test splits across all experiments. For Dialogue Summary: 1,000 train samples (from respective dataset) mixed with 100 PureBad samples, and 1,500 test samples; Alpaca uses 80/20 split with explicit proportions. QA2: Comparison against five baselines: LoRA, SafeInstr, BEA, SafeLoRA, and Vaccine—all clearly evaluated across multiple metrics and datasets. QA3: Complete hyperparameter specification including LoRA rank=8, learning rates (3e-5 to 5e-4 depending on model/dataset), batch sizes (8 or 16), 5 epochs of training, and PEFT-specific parameters (E-DIEM configuration with IQR scaling, threshold values, pruning layers). QA4: All datasets fully characterized: Dialog Summary (abstractive summarization domain, 1,500 test samples), Alpaca (instruction-following domain, 52.2K total with 80/20 split), PureBad (safety evaluation domain, 100 harmful examples). Domain is clearly safety-aligned LoRA fine-tuning for LLMs, a computational technique.

QA1=1: The paper explicitly reports a 80/10/10 split with exact sizes (1909 train, 239 validation, 239 test) from 2387 total dialogues. QA2=0: No baseline comparisons are provided; the study evaluates eight models with three adaptation strategies but does not compare against a baseline model, prior methods, or alternative approaches—only compares models against each other. QA3=0.5: The paper reports basic hyperparameters (Adam optimizer, 450 epochs) but critically lacks learning rate and batch size values. For the three PEFT methods (LoRA, QLoRA, Freeze), no technique-specific parameters are reported (no LoRA rank/alpha values, no QLoRA quantization bit details explicitly stated in methods, no Freeze layer specifications). QA4=1: The dataset is fully characterized with name (CBT-I dialogue dataset), domain/task (cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia treatment), and size (2387 total dialogues with clear breakdown by split). C-eval is also characterized as 13,948 multiple-choice questions in 52 disciplines. This is a medical/clinical NLP application focused on insomnia treatment support.

QA1 (1): The paper explicitly reports the experimental split with exact sample sizes: 150,105 training samples and 17,627 test samples (total 167,732 pairs). QA2 (1): The paper compares against multiple baselines—LLAMA 3 (8B) base model, MedAlpaca, and human expert responses—meeting the criterion for two or more baselines. QA3 (1): Complete hyperparameter set is reported: learning rate 3e-5, batch size 32, 5 epochs, LoRA rank 8, using peft library and bitsandbytes. All technique-specific PEFT parameters (LoRA rank) are explicitly stated in Section 3.2. QA4 (1): The dataset is fully characterized with (a) explicit name and identifier (doktorsitesi.com, 167,732 question-answer pairs), (b) domain and task context (Turkish medical platform with patient-doctor interactions across specialties: cardiology, dermatology, obstetrics, orthopedics, psychiatry), and (c) exact size breakdown (150,105 training, 17,627 test). The paper is classified as "Salud y Biomedicina" because it focuses on clinical NLP applied to Turkish medical contexts, patient-doctor interactions, and healthcare AI systems.

QA1 (1): The paper explicitly reports the evaluation dataset split: "Three months of data from 15 April to 15 July 2024 was crawled from Hellobacsi... consisting of 578 QA pairs. This evaluation dataset was exclusively used for evaluation purposes and was not used in model fine-tuning." The fine-tuning dataset comprises 337,000 prompt-response pairs from three sources (73,000 from existing datasets, ~7,000 from forums, 257,530 from textbooks), clearly delineating train and evaluation splits. QA2 (1): The paper compares fine-tuned models against base models for all three architectures (BloomZ-3B, LLaMA2-7B, LLaMA2-13B), consistently reporting results for both versions across BERTScore, ROUGE-L, and LLM-as-a-Judge metrics. This satisfies the requirement for two or more baselines. QA3 (0.5): While the paper reports learning rate (0.001) and epochs (6), it lacks critical PEFT-specific hyperparameters. For LoRA/QLoRA models, the paper does not explicitly report rank (r) and alpha (α) values. The statement "fine-tuning configuration recommended by Xue et al." provides lr and epochs but no LoRA rank or alpha. This is insufficient for a score of 1 despite basic parameters being present. QA4 (1): The dataset is fully characterized: name/source (ViHealthQA, PubmedQA, HealthMagicQA, medical forums, textbooks), domain (healthcare/medical in Vietnamese, low-resource language context), and size (337,000 prompt-response pairs with breakdown: 73,000 from existing datasets, 7,000 from forums, 257,530 from textbook distillation). All three required elements are explicitly present.

QA1 (1/1): The paper explicitly reports train/test/validation split proportions: "80% is used for baseline model training, 10% of the data is used for model testing, and 10% of the data is used for model validation" with total dataset size of 44,754 samples. QA2 (1/1): The paper compares MoELoRA against five baseline models (Qwen2-7B, ChatGLM3-6B, Llama3-8B, GPT-4) and four fine-tuning methods (Adapter, Prefix-tuning, Prompt-tuning, LoRA), exceeding the requirement of two or more baselines. QA3 (0.5/1): While the paper reports learning rate (lr=2e-5 mentioned in related work context) and provides architectural details, it lacks explicit reporting of critical PEFT-specific hyperparameters for MoELoRA: rank (r), LoRA alpha (α), number of experts (N), batch size, and exact number of training epochs/steps are not provided in a complete hyperparameter table. QA4 (1/1): The dataset is fully characterized: name ("coal mining equipment maintenance dataset"), domain (coal mining equipment maintenance with four subtasks: preventive maintenance, fault diagnosis, repair planning, safety), and size (44,754 total samples with explicit breakdown by task: 10,338 preventive, 10,686 fault diagnosis, 12,206 repair, 11,524 safety).

QA1 (1/1): The paper explicitly reports data splits with exact numbers: development set 95,506 (train), 1,000 (validation), 1,000 (test); AZ validation set 1,000; MIMIC-EchoNotes 1,000. QA2 (1/1): Multiple baselines compared—four open-source LLM models (Llama-2, MedAlpaca, Zephyr, Flan-T5) tested in zero-shot and fine-tuned configurations, plus ICL variants and prior work (EchoGen). QA3 (1/1): Complete hyperparameter reporting: QLoRA config (alpha=16, LoRA rank=64, dropout=0.1), 4-bit precision, batch size 24, learning rate 1e-3 decaying to 1e-4 with cosine scheduler, 100 warmup steps, paged-AdamW optimizer. QA4 (1/1): Datasets fully characterized: (a) Mayo Clinic Reports (97,506 reports from clinical practice 2017), MIMIC-III ECHO-NOTE (43,472 reports from 2001–2012); (b) domain specified as echocardiography clinical reporting; (c) sizes explicitly given. This is clinical/medical AI applied to cardiology report generation.

QA1 (0.5): The paper mentions using GLUE benchmark with a hyperparameter search for learning rates {2e-5, 5e-4} and epochs {3, 20}, but does not explicitly state train/test/validation split proportions or exact sizes for the experimental datasets, only referencing the standard GLUE splits without reporting them. QA2 (1.0): The paper compares AdaptForever against three baseline methods (Adapterd, Adapterh, Adapterp) across multiple tasks and configurations with full performance tables provided. QA3 (0.5): While the paper reports batch sizes (64 for base, 32 for large), learning rate ranges, and epochs (3-20), it lacks explicit reporting of critical PEFT-specific hyperparameters including the number of experts (N) and bottleneck sizes (D) used in the main experiments described in Section 4.1-4.2. Only in Section 4.4 is the exploration of N and D shown in Table 2, but the specific values used for the reported baseline comparisons are not clearly stated in the experimental setup. QA4 (1.0): The paper clearly identifies GLUE benchmark as the dataset, provides the domain context (diverse NLP tasks including textual entailment MNLI, sentiment analysis SST-2, question answering QNLI), and implicitly indicates size through the well-characterized benchmark, though total dataset size could be more explicit.

QA1 (score 1): The paper explicitly reports splitting 2143 QA pairs into training, validation, and test sets at an 8:1:1 ratio (Section 4.2), providing exact proportions. QA2 (score 1): The paper compares the proposed Qwen2.5-LoRA + GraphRAG method against four baseline models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9b-it, GLM-4-9B-Chat, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct baseline) in Table 4, exceeding the minimum two baselines requirement. QA3 (score 1): Table 3 reports a complete hyperparameter configuration including learning_rate (1×10⁻⁴), num_train_epochs (3), gradient_accumulation_steps (4), per_device_train_batch_size (1), and LoRA-specific parameters (lora_rank=8, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05). QA4 (score 1): The dataset is fully characterized with name ("ancient ceramic QA pairs dataset"), domain/task context (ancient ceramics knowledge question-answering in digital cultural heritage), and size (2143 QA pairs after curation, split 8:1:1).

QA1: The paper explicitly reports train/test splits with specific dataset sizes in Table 1 for all three datasets (e.g., FB15K-237: 272,115 train, 17,535 validation, 20,466 test). QA2: Multiple baselines are compared (TransE, TuckER, NBFNet, SimKGC, ChatGPT, KICGPT, CP-KGC, DIFT+CoLE, LLaMA variants) across embedding-based and LLM-based methods, providing comprehensive comparison. QA3: Complete hyperparameter set reported including LoRA-specific parameters (rank r=8, scaling factor α=32, dropout 0.05), learning rate 1×10⁻⁴, batch size 8, 1 epoch, maximum sequence length 4096, plus 4-bit quantization and optimization details. QA4: All three datasets fully characterized: name + domain context (UMLS biomedical, FB15K-237 general domain from Freebase, WN18RR lexical hierarchies from WordNet) + explicit size statistics in Table 1.

QA1 (0.5): The paper mentions splitting data for pre-training and fine-tuning phases but does not explicitly report proportions or exact sizes for the experimental splits. For example, pre-training uses "1.5×10^6 triples" and fine-tuning uses WebQSP (2998 training, 100 dev, 1639 test) and MetaQA (sizes reported in Table 3), but the paper does not clearly specify the train/validation/test split for the pre-training phase on the knowledge graphs themselves. QA2 (1.0): The paper compares against two strong baselines: (1) fine-tuning only on KGQA tasks without knowledge infusion, and (2) infusion with knowledge triples only (without prompt-based unification). Additionally, ablation studies compare against multiple conditions (no unification, task-only prompts, entity-only prompts), and PEFT comparisons include adapter-tuning and LoRA. QA3 (0.5): The pre-training section reports learning rate (4×10^-1 with linear decay), batch sizes (128 for small/base, 64 for large), number of epochs (40 for small/base, 20 for large), optimizer (AdaFactor), and dropout (0.1). However, for the fine-tuning phase on KGQA, the paper explicitly states "no dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning is applied" but does not report the learning rate, batch size, or other hyperparameters used for fine-tuning. For PEFT methods, the paper mentions "default HuggingFace implementations of adapter-tuning and LoRA" without specifying technique-specific parameters (e.g., LoRA rank, alpha, adapter bottleneck size). This is insufficient for a score of 1.0. QA4 (1.0): All datasets are fully characterized: (a) WebQSP is named and described as containing 4737 natural language questions from Freebase with 2-hop reasoning; (b) MetaQA is named, its domain (movie) is specified, and it includes 400,000+ questions broken down by hop type (1-hop: 29,000; 2-hop: 140,000; 3-hop: 140,000), with training/dev/test splits reported in Table 3. Domain: Lenguaje y Humanidades—the paper addresses knowledge graph question answering (KGQA), a general NLP task working with standard benchmarks and natural language reasoning, not domain-specific to health, finance, law, or code.

QA1 (1.0): The paper explicitly reports train/validation/test splits with exact proportions: "Training: 1707 (80%), Validation: 213 (10%), Test: 214 (10%)" in Table 1, meeting the requirement for clear, numerically specified splits. QA2 (1.0): The paper compares against two baseline strategies: (1) zeroshot generation using pretrained models without fine-tuning (Section 3.6), and (2) supervised fine-tuning alone before RL, with results across three different models. Tables 5 and 6 present comprehensive comparisons across three stages (base pretrained, fine-tuned, RL-enhanced). QA3 (1.0): Complete hyperparameter reporting is provided: LoRA rank r=16, alpha α=32, dropout p=0.05 (Section 3.7.4); learning rate 5×10⁻⁵, batch size 8 with gradient accumulation to 32, max steps 1800, optimizer AdamW with weight decay 0.01 (Section 3.7.5); XGBoost engagement model parameters; PPO parameters including clipping range 0.2, entropy coefficient 0.01 (Section 3.10.1). QA4 (1.0): Dataset is fully characterized: name ("Verified NFT Tweets" from Kaggle), domain (NFT-related tweets, 2020-2022), and size details (2134 total after curation, split across engagement levels: Low 725, Medium 710, High 699; training 1707, validation 213, test 214).

QA1 (1): The paper explicitly reports an 8:1:1 train/validation/test split with fixed random seed (Section 3.1: "The dataset was partitioned into training, validation, and test sets at an 8:1:1 ratio"). QA2 (1): The paper compares against two baselines: a LoRA-based Baseline (Section 4.4) and GPT-4o under 0-shot and 3-shot settings (Section 4.4 and Figure 7). QA3 (1): Complete hyperparameter reporting is provided (Section 4.1): batch size 1, gradient accumulation 8, learning rate 2×10⁻⁴, LoRA rank 16, dropout 0.05, 3 epochs, random seed 42, plus PEFT-specific parameters (rank, dropout). QA4 (1): Dataset is fully characterized: name (Bugzilla-based dataset from [27]), domain (open-source bug report generation, software maintenance), and size (3966 summary–report pairs, 8:1:1 split → 3172 train / 397 validation / 397 test).

QA1 (score 1): Section 2.6 explicitly states "stratified five-fold cross validation with 80:20 splits" for T5 fine-tuning, and the same methodology is applied to Zephyr with exact proportions reported. QA2 (score 1): The paper compares fine-tuned T5, fine-tuned Zephyr, zero-shot Zephyr, zero-shot GPT 3.5, and zero-shot GPT 4—multiple baselines across sections 3.3. QA3 (score 1): For Zephyr fine-tuning, the paper explicitly reports learning rate (0.0002), batch size (1), epochs (1), optimizer (paged_adamw_8bit), and QLoRA-specific parameters (4-bit quantization, maximum quantization samples 1024). T5 parameters are referenced to [32]. QA4 (score 1): The dataset is fully characterized: name (multi-source corpus from PubMed, ADECorpus, SMM4H, drugs.com), domain (pharmacovigilance NER with adverse event/drug/dose/indication entities), and size (890 records total, 500 from ADE Corpus used in model selection experiments).

QA1=1: The paper explicitly reports train/test split with exact sizes: 6097 notes randomly selected for annotation, 3000 designated as test set, 3097 plus 3000 additional notes comprising validation set (Figure 1 and text). QA2=0.5: The paper compares three fine-tuned models (Llama 2 7B, Mistral 7B, Mixtral 8×7B) against each other but lacks comparison with external baselines or prior published deidentification methods, making it a single-method evaluation across model variants. QA3=1: Complete hyperparameter reporting includes learning rate (5e-5), batch sizes (24 for Llama 2/Mistral, 20 for Mixtral), epochs (15), optimizer (AdamW), weight decay (0.01), and PEFT-specific LoRA parameters: rank=32, alpha=64, dropout=0.1, quantization (8-bit for 7B models, 4-bit for Mixtral). QA4=1: Dataset fully characterized with name/identifier (425,680 clinical notes from Bordeaux University Hospital emergency department), domain/task context (clinical deidentification for emergency department triage notes, 2013-2022), and size breakdown (3000 test, 6097 total annotated, 425,680 source repository).

QA1 (0.5): Split is mentioned ("only sample around 20% of the training set and 2% of the test set") but lacks explicit proportions for train/validation/test or total dataset sizes in absolute numbers. QA2 (1.0): Comparison against two baselines: FedIT [15] and FedPTuning [16], with results reported in Figures 3 and Table I. QA3 (0.5): Learning rate, batch size (8), and number of communication rounds (60) are provided. However, LoRA-specific parameters are incompletely reported: rank r is varied {4,8,16} with r=16 selected, but α (alpha) is discussed theoretically as "functionally equivalent to optimizing the learning rate" without explicit numerical value. Optimizer type (Adam) is mentioned but not full configuration. QA4 (1.0): Two datasets fully characterized: (a) Natural Instructions (NI) with domain (NLP instruction-following tasks), size (20% of training, 2% of test sampled, 80 clients); (b) Dolly-15k with domain (instruction-tuned LLM dataset), and size (80 clients). Both datasets include name, domain context, and size specifications. Domain classification: LLM fine-tuning, federated learning, and parameter-efficient tuning are core computational topics without clinical or biomedical focus.

QA1: The paper explicitly reports train/validation/test splits with exact proportions: 90% of data for training/validation (80% train, 10% validation) and 10% for testing, applied to ~12,000 tweets per model after augmentation (~9,600 train, 1,200 validation, 1,200 test). QA2: The paper compares fine-tuned Flan-T5 against exactly one baseline—the pre-trained Flan-T5 model (accuracy 0.33 vs 0.91 for tobacco intent, 0.36 vs 0.93 for e-cigarette intent, 0.65 vs 0.94 for sentiment). No comparison with other fine-tuning methods or alternative baselines is provided. QA3: Table 5 provides a complete hyperparameter configuration including LoRA-specific parameters (rank=64, alpha=64, dropout=0.05), learning rate (3e-4), batch size (32), number of epochs (10), optimizer (AdamW), evaluation frequency, early stopping criteria (3-epoch patience), and monitoring metric (validation F1). QA4: The paper fully characterizes datasets with (1) names/identifiers (Tobacco Intent LLM, E-cigarette Intent LLM, Sentiment LLM datasets; also COP9 real-world tweets), (2) domain context (tobacco and e-cigarette-related social media sentiment analysis and intent classification for public health research), and (3) explicit sizes (3,000 original tweets per dataset augmented to ~12,000; COP9 dataset: 347 sentiment tweets, 207 tobacco intent, 131 e-cigarette intent).

QA1 (1): The paper explicitly specifies train/test splits for the Alpaca dataset (52,000 instructions used across models, trained for 1 epoch), and clearly states separate hyperparameters and configurations for each model. QA2 (0): No baseline comparisons are made. The paper presents results for fine-tuned models with different optimization combinations but does not compare against a base model without fine-tuning or alternative fine-tuning methods. QA3 (1): Complete hyperparameter reporting is provided. For each model (Phi-3, LLaMA-3.1, Gemma-2B), the paper explicitly reports: learning rate (0.0003 or 0.00002), batch size (2), gradient accumulation steps (16 or 64), optimizer (AdamW) with weight decay, epochs (1), and PEFT-specific parameters (LoRA rank 8/64 and alpha 16/128). QA4 (1): The Alpaca dataset is fully characterized: name ("Alpaca dataset"), domain (general instruction-following for fine-tuning), and size (52,000 instructions/demonstrations). Evaluation used Sycophancy Evaluation Benchmark with explicit accuracy improvements reported (2-5% gains).

QA1: The paper explicitly reports train/validation/test splits for the SFT dataset (28,484 train / 500 validation / 1,000 test) and for the contrastive dataset (6,166 SO-SO / 36,366 SO-Par / 55,494 Par-Par comparisons). QA2: Only one baseline is compared—the base Llama model without fine-tuning (GP Llama). SFT and RLHF variants are ablations of the proposed method, not independent baselines. QA3: Complete hyperparameter sets are reported across all three phases: Classification (LR 5.0e-5, batch size 256, dropout 0.3), LoRA finetuning for SFT (rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.1, LR 1.0e-4), and RLHF with PPO (LR 1.41e-5, target KL 6, GAE λ 0.95, batch size 64, 10 epochs). QA4: Stack Overflow data fully characterized with name, domain (Python programming Q&A), and sizes (153,914 questions, 256,624 answers; SFT subset: 28,484 train / 500 val / 1,000 test).

QA1 (1): The paper explicitly reports 10-fold cross-validation with stratified sampling: "we performed stratified sampling of each training fold from 363,861 to 100,000 question pairs (comprising 36,920 similar and 63,080 dissimilar pairs)" and "kept the same size of each test fold." QA2 (1): The paper compares against multiple baselines including three state-of-the-art NLP models (SimCSE, MirrorBERT, S-CNN) and four pre-trained LLMs (Alpaca-LoRA-7B, Alpaca-LoRA-65B, LLaMA-7B, LLaMA-33B), plus n-shot variants. QA3 (1): Complete hyperparameters are explicitly reported: "batch size of 128 and ten epochs," "learning rate of 3e-4, lora_r set to 8, lora_alpha set to 16, lora_dropout rate of 0.05," plus inference parameters (temperature=0.1, top_p=0.75, top_k=40, num_beams=4). QA4 (1): The QQP dataset is fully characterized: name (Quora Question Pairs), domain/task context (question pair duplicate identification, part of GLUE benchmark), and size (404,290 total pairs: 255,027 non-duplicates, 149,263 duplicates).

QA1 (score 1): Table 2 explicitly reports train/test/validation splits with exact sample counts: Train (103,395 + 113,281 = 216,676), Test (22,153 + 22,126 = 44,279), Validation (22,167 + 22,143 = 44,310), totaling 305,265 samples. QA2 (score 1): The paper compares fine-tuned models (Qwen2-FT, Minicpm3-FT) against multiple baselines including BERT, BERT-CNN, BERT-DPCNN, BERT-RCNN, BERT-RNN, ERNIE, and non-fine-tuned versions of Qwen2 and Minicpm3 (Table 5). QA3 (score 1): Table 4 provides complete LoRA-specific hyperparameters for both models including rank (8), lora_alpha (16), batch_size (2/8), learning_rate (5×10⁻⁵), lora_dropout (0.01), warmup_steps (10), and gradient_accumulation (24/16). QA4 (score 1): The paper characterizes the instruction dataset (DGI-Corpus) with name, domain/task context (Chinese disaster geospatial intelligence extraction across multiple disaster types), and size (305,265 total samples broken down by split and disaster type in Table 2). Additional datasets are described in Table 3 with names, sources, disaster types, and sample counts.

QA1: The paper explicitly reports dataset splits with exact sizes. For Hook and Bait Urdu: 62,727 training (80%) and 15,682 testing (20%); for ISOT: 35,919 training and 8,979 testing. Table 2 provides detailed class-wise breakdown. QA2: Extensive baseline comparisons are provided. Table 4 compares against 6 Urdu FND benchmarks (Bend the Truth, UrduFake@FIRE 2020/2021, Urdu FND, Ax-to-Grind). Table 5 compares against 4 multilingual/cross-lingual FND approaches covering English+Chinese, English+Dravidian, English+Bengali, and English+Chinese COVID datasets. QA3: Complete hyperparameter reporting including learning rate (2e-5), batch size (16), epochs (5), LoRA rank (4), LoRA alpha (8), LoRA dropout (0.05), optimizer (AdamW), epsilon value, sequence length (512), and early stopping. All PEFT-specific parameters (rank and alpha) are explicitly reported in the experimental implementation details section. QA4: Both datasets fully characterized: (a) Hook and Bait Urdu with name, domain (domain-agnostic fake news detection covering 15 domains), size (78,409 total: 42,179 true, 36,230 fake); (b) ISOT Fake News with name, domain (English multi-domain fake news), size (44,898 total: 21,417 true, 23,481 fake).

QA1 (1): The paper explicitly reports both train and test splits. For summary reports: 560 cases for fine-tuning with 10 entirely independent test cases. For physician letters: 14,479 letters for training with 10 independent test cases. Exact numbers are stated: "Ten entirely independent cases, not included in the training dataset, were set aside for testing." QA2 (0.5): The paper compares the fine-tuned model against exactly one baseline—the non-fine-tuned LLaMA-2 base model (shown in Figure 1). No comparison with other PEFT methods or alternative fine-tuning approaches is provided. QA3 (1): Complete hyperparameter reporting is present, including technique-specific LoRA parameters. Stated values: learning rate 1×10⁻⁵, batch size 2 per GPU, gradient accumulation 2, LoRA rank r=32, scaling factor 64, dropout 0.05, target weight matrices specified (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj, lm_head), 8-bit paged AdamW optimizer, 500 iterations for summary reports and 15,000 for physician letters. QA4 (1): All three required elements are present: (a) dataset name/identifier: physician letters from University Hospital Erlangen 2010-2023; (b) domain and task context: "physician letter generation" and "patient case summary reports" in radiation oncology; (c) size: 14,479 letters for fine-tuning and 10 cases for testing (also 560 cases for summary report task). Domain classification: This is clinical NLP applied to radiation oncology with privacy-preserving local deployment using patient medical data.

QA1 (0): No explicit train/test split sizes are reported. The paper evaluates quantized models on standard benchmarks (WikiText2, C4, PTB, PIQA, etc.) but does not explicitly state how these datasets were partitioned. The statement "To ensure fairness... we set WikiText2 as the calibration dataset... with a sample size of 128 and a sequence length of 2048" refers only to calibration data size, not train/test splits. QA2 (1): The paper extensively compares multiple quantization methods (RTN, GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, QuIP, PB-LLM, DB-LLM, BiLLM, SliM-LLM for PTQ; QLoRA, IR-QLoRA for LoRA-FT)—more than two baselines across three distinct evaluation tracks. QA3 (0.5): For PTQ methods, the paper provides bit-width parameters (#W, #A, #G) but lacks full hyperparameter details such as learning rate or optimization settings—these are evaluation-only methods. For LoRA-FT methods, it states "we fine-tune all models using the same training data and consistent hyperparameters, including learning rate, batch size, number of training epochs, and LoRA configurations such as rank and scaling factors," but no specific numerical values are explicitly reported in the paper. QA4 (1): All datasets are fully characterized. Examples: "WikiText2 [calibration dataset] with a sample size of 128 and sequence length of 2048"; "five zero-shot evaluation tasks (PIQA, Winogrande, ARC-e, ARC-c, HellaSwag)"; "5 visual language benchmarks (AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, MME, and MMBench(English))"; "5-shot MMLU benchmark." Each dataset name and task context are provided with sufficient characterization.

QA1 (Score 1): Experimental split sizes are explicitly reported for all three datasets. IMDB: "25 k training, 25 k val, 50 k test"; Rotten Tomatoes: "9 k Training row, 1 k val, 1 k test"; Emotions: "16k training rows, 2 k val, 2 k test". QA2 (Score 1): The paper compares multiple baselines including centralized training, FedAvg, FedProx, FedNorm, FedFOLB, FedLoss, FedFull, and compares PEFT methods (LoRA, BitFit, QLoRA, IA3, full fine-tuning) within FedAvg. QA3 (Score 0.5): Learning rate (2e-5 mentioned in abstract), batch size (16 mentioned in text), and SGD optimizer are reported.
